questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: In the OSI reference model, which layer is responsible for routing a packet from one network to another through intermediate routers?
questions.question_html:
Question 1MCQeasyosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsstandard textbookMarks: 1

In the OSI reference model, which layer is responsible for routing a packet from one network to another through intermediate routers?
options: Physical layer
Data link layer
Network layer
Transport layer
options_html: APhysical layer
BData link layer
CNetwork layer
DTransport layer
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The OSI layers divide work by scope: the physical layer moves bits, the data link layer moves frames across a single link, the network layer moves packets across a sequence of links, and the transport layer moves data between processes.

Step by step.

  1. Routing means choosing the next hop for a packet whose source and destination lie in different networks.
  2. That decision needs a global (network-wide) address, which is exactly what the network layer provides.
  3. The data link layer only addresses the next machine on the same link; the transport layer does not see routers at all.

Answer: Option (C) — the network layer.

Common misconception. Many candidates choose the transport layer because it is the first ‘end-to-end’ layer. End-to-end delivery is transport; routing inside the network is network layer.

Takeaway. Fix the vocabulary early: routing and logical addressing → network layer; framing and MAC addressing → data link; process-to-process delivery → transport.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which one of the following is NOT a layer of the TCP/IP reference model?
questions.question_html:
Question 2MCQeasyosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which one of the following is NOT a layer of the TCP/IP reference model?
options: Application
Transport
Session
Internet
options_html: AApplication
BTransport
CSession
DInternet
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The TCP/IP reference model has four layers — application, transport, internet and network access (host-to-network).

Step by step.

  1. The application layer merges the OSI application, presentation and session functions.
  2. Transport and internet are layers in their own right.
  3. There is no separate session layer; session-style services (dialogue control, checkpointing) are either omitted or pushed into the application.

Answer: Option (C) — Session.

Common misconception. Candidates who memorise ‘seven layers’ often assume the session layer exists in every model. It is an OSI-only layer.

Takeaway. OSI = 7 layers (physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application). TCP/IP = 4 (or 5 if the link layer is split into link and physical).

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A switch that forwards frames by looking up 48-bit MAC addresses operates at which OSI layer?
questions.question_html:
Question 3MCQeasyosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A switch that forwards frames by looking up 48-bit MAC addresses operates at which OSI layer?
options: Physical layer
Data link layer
Network layer
Transport layer
options_html: APhysical layer
BData link layer
CNetwork layer
DTransport layer
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Device class follows the header the device reads. A MAC address is a data link layer address, so a MAC-address switch is a layer-2 device.

Step by step.

  1. The switch receives a frame, reads its destination MAC address, and forwards it out of the port learned for that address.
  2. It does not modify or inspect the IP header, so it never reaches layer 3.
  3. A hub, by contrast, only repeats electrical signals and is a layer-1 device; a router reads IP addresses and is a layer-3 device.

Answer: Option (B) — the data link layer.

Common misconception. Switches are sometimes called ‘layer-3 switches’ when they also route, which makes candidates assume all switches are layer 3. Plain MAC forwarding is layer 2.

Takeaway. Hub → layer 1, switch/bridge → layer 2, router → layer 3, and a device is named after the highest header it actually processes.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about layering and encapsulation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 4MSQmediumosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about layering and encapsulation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A router forwards a packet using the destination network-layer address and normally does not inspect the transport-layer header.
The data link layer appends a trailer to the frame, while the network layer adds only a header.
A hub regenerates and repeats bits, so it operates at the physical layer.
A protocol converter that works at the application layer is, by definition, a layer-3 device.
options_html: AA router forwards a packet using the destination network-layer address and normally does not inspect the transport-layer header.
BThe data link layer appends a trailer to the frame, while the network layer adds only a header.
CA hub regenerates and repeats bits, so it operates at the physical layer.
DA protocol converter that works at the application layer is, by definition, a layer-3 device.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each layer adds its own control information and reads only its own header; a router is a layer-3 relay and is transparent to transport headers.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — routing needs only the network-layer destination address; the transport header travels untouched.
  2. (B) True — a data link frame carries a trailer (the frame check sequence); the network header has no trailer.
  3. (C) True — a hub performs no frame parsing at all, so it is layer 1.
  4. (D) False — an application-layer converter works at layer 7; a ‘gateway’ in the general sense can operate at any layer.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Statement (D) is the trap: the word ‘gateway’ is sometimes used for a router (layer 3), but an application-level converter is a layer-7 device. The definition in (D) is simply wrong.

Takeaway. Ask of any claim ‘which header does this entity have to read?’ — the answer fixes its layer.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements comparing the OSI and TCP/IP reference models are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 5MSQmediumosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements comparing the OSI and TCP/IP reference models are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The TCP/IP application layer performs the functions that OSI splits across its session, presentation and application layers.
The TCP/IP internet layer corresponds to the OSI network layer.
The TCP/IP reference model has seven layers.
The OSI model was designed before the protocols that implement it existed, whereas the TCP/IP model was written up after its protocols were already in use.
options_html: AThe TCP/IP application layer performs the functions that OSI splits across its session, presentation and application layers.
BThe TCP/IP internet layer corresponds to the OSI network layer.
CThe TCP/IP reference model has seven layers.
DThe OSI model was designed before the protocols that implement it existed, whereas the TCP/IP model was written up after its protocols were already in use.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. OSI is a protocol-independent architecture written first; TCP/IP is a description of an already-working protocol suite.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — presentation (encoding, compression, encryption) and session services are handled inside application protocols in TCP/IP.
  2. (B) True — the internet layer provides logical addressing and routing, exactly the OSI network layer's job.
  3. (C) False — TCP/IP has four layers (five if the link layer is split).
  4. (D) True — the classic historical distinction: OSI came from a model, TCP/IP came from running code.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Statement (C) is the usual error, produced by carrying the OSI count over to TCP/IP. Also note (D) is a genuine, examinable distinction, not trivia.

Takeaway. Two facts to keep: TCP/IP = 4 layers and no session/presentation layer; OSI = 7 layers and model-first.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An application message of 600 bytes is passed down the stack. The transport layer adds a 20-byte header, the network layer adds a 20-byte header, and the data link layer adds a 14-byte header and a 4-byte trailer. What is the total size, in bytes, of the frame handed to the physical layer?
questions.question_html:
Question 6NATeasyosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

An application message of 600 bytes is passed down the stack. The transport layer adds a 20-byte header, the network layer adds a 20-byte header, and the data link layer adds a 14-byte header and a 4-byte trailer.
What is the total size, in bytes, of the frame handed to the physical layer?

Answer format: an integer number of bytes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Encapsulation adds one header at each layer (and a trailer at the data link layer), so the sizes simply add.

Step by step.

  1. Application data: 600 bytes.
  2. Transport segment: 600 + 20 = 620 bytes.
  3. Network datagram: 620 + 20 = 640 bytes.
  4. Data link frame: 640 + 14 + 4 = 658 bytes.

Answer: 658 bytes.

Common misconception. The common slip is to forget the 4-byte trailer, or to add the transport header twice because the segment is later called a payload. Overhead here is 58 bytes in total.

Takeaway. Layer overhead is cumulative: every header added below is carried by everything above it.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A frame travels from a source host to a destination host through two routers. Which statement about error checking on this path is correct?
questions.question_html:
Question 7MCQhardosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A frame travels from a source host to a destination host through two routers. Which statement about error checking on this path is correct?
options: Both the frame check sequence and the TCP checksum are verified only at the destination host.
The frame check sequence is verified by every device that receives the frame, including each router; the TCP checksum is verified only at the destination host.
The frame check sequence is verified only at the destination host; the TCP checksum is verified at every router.
Both the frame check sequence and the TCP checksum are verified at every router along the path.
options_html: ABoth the frame check sequence and the TCP checksum are verified only at the destination host.
BThe frame check sequence is verified by every device that receives the frame, including each router; the TCP checksum is verified only at the destination host.
CThe frame check sequence is verified only at the destination host; the TCP checksum is verified at every router.
DBoth the frame check sequence and the TCP checksum are verified at every router along the path.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Error detection is layered, and each layer's check has the scope of that layer: a data link check covers one hop, a transport check covers the whole end-to-end path.

Step by step.

  1. When a router receives a frame it recomputes the frame check sequence over the received bits; a bad frame is discarded on that hop.
  2. The router then strips the data link header and trailer, so the next hop gets a brand-new frame with a newly computed check sequence.
  3. The TCP header and its checksum travel end to end untouched, so only the destination transport layer can verify them — a router never even looks at them.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. The tempting error is (D): students reason that ‘every device checks for errors’. A router cannot verify a TCP checksum without reassembling the transport segment, which it does not do.

Takeaway. Per-hop check ⇒ data link; end-to-end check ⇒ transport. This is the cleanest illustration of why both layers exist.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A 1500-byte packet is placed on a 1 Mbps link. Ignoring propagation, processing and queueing delay, what is the transmission delay?
questions.question_html:
Question 8MCQeasytransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productstandard textbookMarks: 1

A 1500-byte packet is placed on a 1 Mbps link. Ignoring propagation, processing and queueing delay, what is the transmission delay?
options: 1.2 ms
12 ms
120 ms
options_html: A1.2 ms
B12 ms
C120 ms
D0.12 ms
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Transmission delay is the time to push all the bits of the packet onto the link: L / R, with L in bits and R in bits per second.

Step by step.

  1. L = 1500 bytes = 1500 × 8 = 12000 bits.
  2. R = 1 Mbps = 10⁶ bits per second.
  3. L / R = 12000 / 10⁶ = 0.012 s = 12 ms.

Answer: Option (B) — 12 ms.

Common misconception. Forgetting the factor of 8 (bytes to bits) gives 1.5 ms or 1.2 ms, which is why those distractors are present.

Takeaway. Always convert to bits before dividing by a bit rate: delay = 8 × size_in_bytes / bandwidth.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Two links have the same length and the same propagation speed, but link 1 has twice the bandwidth of link 2. For the same packet, which of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html:
Question 9MCQeasytransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Two links have the same length and the same propagation speed, but link 1 has twice the bandwidth of link 2. For the same packet, which of the following is TRUE?
options: The propagation delay is the same on both links, and the transmission delay is smaller on link 1.
Both delays are smaller on link 1.
The transmission delay is the same on both links, and the propagation delay is smaller on link 1.
Both delays are the same on both links.
options_html: AThe propagation delay is the same on both links, and the transmission delay is smaller on link 1.
BBoth delays are smaller on link 1.
CThe transmission delay is the same on both links, and the propagation delay is smaller on link 1.
DBoth delays are the same on both links.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Transmission delay depends on the link's bandwidth; propagation delay depends only on distance and signal speed.

Step by step.

  1. Propagation delay = distance / propagation speed, and both are identical, so the two links have equal propagation delay.
  2. Transmission delay = L / R; R is doubled on link 1, so its transmission delay is halved.
  3. Therefore only the transmission delay changes.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. The frequent error is (B): assuming a ‘faster link’ shortens everything. Bandwidth cannot make a signal travel faster than the propagation speed of the medium.

Takeaway. Bandwidth governs how long the packet takes to enter the wire; distance governs how long it takes to cross it.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A link has a bandwidth of 100 Mbps and a one-way propagation delay of 20 ms. What is the bandwidth-delay product of the link, in kilobytes? Use 1 kB = 1000 bytes and enter a number.
questions.question_html:
Question 10NATmediumtransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A link has a bandwidth of 100 Mbps and a one-way propagation delay of 20 ms.
What is the bandwidth-delay product of the link, in kilobytes? Use 1 kB = 1000 bytes and enter a number.

Answer format: a number in kB (1 kB = 1000 bytes).
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth × propagation delay. It is the number of bits that can be in flight on the link at one instant.

Step by step.

  1. R = 100 Mbps = 10⁸ bits/s; delay = 20 ms = 0.02 s.
  2. BDP = 10⁸ × 0.02 = 2 × 10⁶ bits.
  3. In bytes: 2 × 10⁶ / 8 = 250000 bytes.
  4. In kB (1000 bytes): 250000 / 1000 = 250 kB.

Answer: 250 kB.

Common misconception. Two errors dominate: dividing by 1024 instead of 1000, and using bits per byte wrongly, giving 244 or 2000. The question fixes 1 kB = 1000 bytes to remove the first ambiguity.

Takeaway. BDP answers ‘how much data must be outstanding to keep the pipe full?’ — the basis of the TCP window sizing question.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Two hosts are 3000 km apart on a link whose signal propagates at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the one-way propagation delay?
questions.question_html:
Question 11MCQeasytransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Two hosts are 3000 km apart on a link whose signal propagates at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the one-way propagation delay?
options: 1 ms
10 ms
100 ms
0.1 ms
options_html: A1 ms
B10 ms
C100 ms
D0.1 ms
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Propagation delay = distance / propagation speed.

Step by step.

  1. Distance = 3000 km = 3 × 10⁶ m.
  2. Speed = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  3. Delay = 3 × 10⁶ / 3 × 10⁸ = 10⁻² s = 10 ms.

Answer: Option (B) — 10 ms.

Common misconception. A kilometre-to-metre slip (using 3000 m) gives 0.01 ms, and a factor-of-ten slip gives 100 ms. Both appear as options.

Takeaway. Keep units consistent: convert km to m before dividing by m/s, and remember 10⁻³ s = 1 ms.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about delay, bandwidth and the bandwidth-delay product are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 12MSQhardtransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about delay, bandwidth and the bandwidth-delay product are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The bandwidth-delay product of a link equals the maximum number of bits that can be in transit on that link at any instant.
Doubling the propagation delay and halving the bandwidth leaves the bandwidth-delay product unchanged.
The transmission delay of a packet depends on the distance between the two end hosts.
The throughput of a path is limited by the slowest link on it, while the end-to-end delay is the sum of the per-link delays.
options_html: AThe bandwidth-delay product of a link equals the maximum number of bits that can be in transit on that link at any instant.
BDoubling the propagation delay and halving the bandwidth leaves the bandwidth-delay product unchanged.
CThe transmission delay of a packet depends on the distance between the two end hosts.
DThe throughput of a path is limited by the slowest link on it, while the end-to-end delay is the sum of the per-link delays.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. BDP = R × Tprop is the ‘amount of pipe’; transmission delay is L / R; throughput of a path is set by the bottleneck link.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — that is the definition: the bits that fit inside the link while the first bit is still travelling.
  2. (B) True — (R/2) × (2T) = R × T.
  3. (C) False — transmission delay is L / R and contains no distance term; it is the propagation delay that depends on distance.
  4. (D) True — for a single flow the sustained rate cannot exceed the minimum link rate, and the delays add up hop by hop.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Statement (C) is the standard confusion between the two delays. A satellite link of huge length but high bandwidth still has a tiny transmission delay and a large propagation delay.

Takeaway. Transmission delay: packet size vs bandwidth. Propagation delay: distance vs signal speed. Never mix them.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A 1000-byte packet is sent from a source to a destination over three links in series, each of bandwidth 1 Mbps. The switches are store-and-forward and propagation delay is negligible. What is the total time from the first bit leaving the source to the last bit arriving at the destination?
questions.question_html:
Question 13MCQmediumtransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productstandard textbookMarks: 1

A 1000-byte packet is sent from a source to a destination over three links in series, each of bandwidth 1 Mbps. The switches are store-and-forward and propagation delay is negligible. What is the total time from the first bit leaving the source to the last bit arriving at the destination?
options: 8 ms
16 ms
24 ms
32 ms
options_html: A8 ms
B16 ms
C24 ms
D32 ms
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Under store-and-forward, a switch must receive the whole packet before it can begin transmitting it on the next link, so each hop costs one full transmission time.

Step by step.

  1. One transmission time = 1000 × 8 / 10⁶ = 8 ms.
  2. The source pushes the packet onto link 1 in 8 ms; the packet then needs 8 ms on link 2 and 8 ms on link 3.
  3. Total = 3 × 8 = 24 ms.

Answer: Option (C) — 24 ms.

Common misconception. The popular wrong answer is 8 ms, from imagining that the bits flow continuously through all three links at once. That is cut-through switching, not store-and-forward.

Takeaway. Store-and-forward over k equal links: total = k × L/R (plus propagation). Only the first hop overlaps with nothing.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Why is bit stuffing used in a bit-oriented framing protocol such as HDLC?
questions.question_html:
Question 14MCQeasyframing-bit-byte-stuffingstandard textbookMarks: 1

Why is bit stuffing used in a bit-oriented framing protocol such as HDLC?
options: To make sure the flag pattern 01111110 never appears inside the data.
To detect bit errors introduced by the channel.
To compress the data before transmission.
To keep the receiver's clock synchronised with the sender's.
options_html: ATo make sure the flag pattern 01111110 never appears inside the data.
BTo detect bit errors introduced by the channel.
CTo compress the data before transmission.
DTo keep the receiver's clock synchronised with the sender's.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Framing needs an unambiguous delimiter. If the delimiter could occur in the payload, the receiver could not tell data from a frame boundary.

Step by step.

  1. HDLC uses the flag 01111110 at the start and end of every frame.
  2. A payload containing six consecutive 1s would imitate that flag.
  3. The sender therefore inserts a 0 after every five consecutive 1s, so six 1s can never occur inside a frame.
  4. The receiver deletes the inserted 0 again.

Answer: Option (A) — transparency of the flag.

Common misconception. Bit stuffing is often confused with error detection (option B). HDLC detects errors with the frame check sequence; stuffing only guarantees frame transparency.

Takeaway. Framing problems are solved by transparency mechanisms (stuffing, escaping), never by checksums.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: In byte-oriented framing, FLAG = 0x7E and ESC = 0x7D, and the escape rule is to transmit ESC followed by the data byte XORed with 0x20. How is a data byte 0x7D transmitted?
questions.question_html:
Question 15MCQeasyframing-bit-byte-stuffingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

In byte-oriented framing, FLAG = 0x7E and ESC = 0x7D, and the escape rule is to transmit ESC followed by the data byte XORed with 0x20. How is a data byte 0x7D transmitted?
options: 0x7D 0x7D
0x7D 0x5D
0x5D
0x7E 0x7D
options_html: A0x7D 0x7D
B0x7D 0x5D
C0x5D
D0x7E 0x7D
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every occurrence of the flag byte and of the escape byte itself must be escaped, so the receiver never mistakes data for a delimiter.

Step by step.

  1. The data byte is 0x7D, which equals ESC.
  2. XOR with 0x20: 0x7D ⊕ 0x20 = 0x5D.
  3. Transmit ESC first, then the escaped byte: 0x7D 0x5D.

Answer: Option (B) — 0x7D 0x5D.

Common misconception. Many candidates escape only the flag. Forgetting that the escape byte itself must be escaped makes the receiver treat a data 0x7D as the start of an escape sequence.

Takeaway. Two bytes need escaping in byte stuffing: the flag and the escape byte itself. The XOR with 0x20 flips bit 5, which maps 0x7E→0x5E and 0x7D→0x5D.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A frame uses byte stuffing with FLAG = 0x7E and ESC = 0x7D; an escape sequence is ESC followed by the data byte XORed with 0x20. The data to be transmitted is the six-byte sequence 41 7E 7D 42 7E 43 (hex). How many bytes are transmitted between the two flags?
questions.question_html:
Question 16NATmediumframing-bit-byte-stuffingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A frame uses byte stuffing with FLAG = 0x7E and ESC = 0x7D; an escape sequence is ESC followed by the data byte XORed with 0x20. The data to be transmitted is the six-byte sequence
41 7E 7D 42 7E 43 (hex).
How many bytes are transmitted between the two flags?

Answer format: an integer number of bytes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Byte stuffing replaces each occurrence of FLAG or ESC by a two-byte escape sequence; every other byte passes through unchanged.

Step by step.

  1. 0x41 is neither FLAG nor ESC → 0x41 (1 byte).
  2. 0x7E = FLAG → 0x7D 0x5E (2 bytes).
  3. 0x7D = ESC → 0x7D 0x5D (2 bytes).
  4. 0x42 → 0x42 (1 byte).
  5. 0x7E → 0x7D 0x5E (2 bytes).
  6. 0x43 → 0x43 (1 byte).
  7. Total = 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 9 bytes.

Answer: 9 bytes.

Common misconception. The usual mistakes are escaping only the two FLAG bytes (giving 8) or forgetting that the ESC byte must itself be escaped (giving 8 as well, but for a different reason).

Takeaway. Count the growth: each escaped byte adds exactly one byte to the frame, so the payload grows from 6 to 9.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The data bit stream 011111101111101111110 is to be transmitted with bit stuffing, where a 0 is inserted after every five consecutive 1s. How many bits are inserted?
questions.question_html:
Question 17MCQmediumframing-bit-byte-stuffingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

The data bit stream 011111101111101111110 is to be transmitted with bit stuffing, where a 0 is inserted after every five consecutive 1s. How many bits are inserted?
options_html: A2
B3
C4
D5
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Scan the stream keeping a running count of consecutive 1s; whenever the count reaches five, insert a 0 and reset the counter.

Step by step.

  1. Group 1: the leading 0111111 has six consecutive 1s → one 0 inserted after the fifth 1.
  2. The inserted 0 resets the run, so the sixth 1 starts a new run of length 1.
  3. Group 2: 11111 → one 0 inserted.
  4. Group 3: 111111 → one 0 inserted after the fifth 1.
  5. Total insertions = 3.

Answer: Option (B) — 3 bits.

Common misconception. The trap is to treat a run of six 1s as a single insertion of two 0s, or to stop counting once a 0 has been inserted. Each insertion resets the counter, and each new run of five earns its own insertion.

Takeaway. Work left to right with a counter, never by eye: after inserting a 0 the run length is 0, and the next bit restarts it.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about framing techniques are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 18MSQmediumframing-bit-byte-stuffingstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about framing techniques are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: In byte-oriented framing, only the flag byte and the escape byte itself need to be escaped.
In bit-oriented framing, the receiver removes a 0 that immediately follows five consecutive 1s.
Character-count framing keeps synchronisation even if the count field of a frame is corrupted.
In character-count framing, a corrupted count field destroys the framing of all the following frames in the stream.
options_html: AIn byte-oriented framing, only the flag byte and the escape byte itself need to be escaped.
BIn bit-oriented framing, the receiver removes a 0 that immediately follows five consecutive 1s.
CCharacter-count framing keeps synchronisation even if the count field of a frame is corrupted.
DIn character-count framing, a corrupted count field destroys the framing of all the following frames in the stream.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. There are three standard framing methods: character count, flag bytes with stuffing, and flag bits with bit stuffing. Each has a different failure mode.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — any other byte value can appear in the data without ambiguity, so only FLAG and ESC need escaping.
  2. (B) True — that is exactly the de-stuffing rule, and it is what makes six 1s impossible inside a frame.
  3. (C) False and (D) True — the count field tells the receiver where the frame ends, so a corrupted count shifts every subsequent boundary. This is the classic weakness of character-count framing.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Statements (C) and (D) are contradictory, so one must be false: candidates who pick both have not modelled what the receiver does with the count.

Takeaway. Character count: simple, but one bad count desynchronises the stream. Flag-based methods recover because the receiver can rescan for the next flag.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The data stream 01111101111110 is transmitted with bit stuffing (a 0 is inserted after every five consecutive 1s). Which is the transmitted stream?
questions.question_html:
Question 19MCQhardframing-bit-byte-stuffingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

The data stream 01111101111110 is transmitted with bit stuffing (a 0 is inserted after every five consecutive 1s). Which is the transmitted stream?
options_html: A0111110111111010
B01111100111111010
C0111110011111010
D011111001111010
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Bit stuffing is applied left to right with a counter of consecutive 1s; each insertion adds a 0 and resets the counter.

Step by step.

  1. Original: 0 1 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 (14 bits).
  2. Bits 2–6 are five 1s → insert 0 after bit 6.
  3. Bit 7 is 0; then bits 8–12 are five 1s → insert 0 after bit 12.
  4. Bit 13 is 1 (a new run of length 1) and bit 14 is 0, so no further insertion.
  5. Result: 0 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 1 1 1 1 1 0 1 0 = 0111110011111010 (16 bits).

Answer: Option (C) — 0111110011111010.

Common misconception. Option (A) is the original stream with two 0s appended, and option (B) has 17 bits because a 0 was inserted after a run of only four 1s. Both come from stuffing by eye rather than by counter.

Takeaway. Write the output bit by bit and keep the counter visible; the length grows by exactly the number of insertions.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: What is the Hamming distance between the two 7-bit codewords 1011101 and 1001001?
questions.question_html:
Question 20MCQeasyerror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingstandard textbookMarks: 1

What is the Hamming distance between the two 7-bit codewords 1011101 and 1001001?
options_html: A1
B2
C3
D4
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The Hamming distance is the number of bit positions in which the two codewords differ.

Step by step.

  1. Align the words: 1 0 1 1 1 0 1 and 1 0 0 1 0 0 1.
  2. Position 1: 1 = 1. Position 2: 0 = 0. Position 3: 1 ≠ 0. Position 4: 1 = 1.
  3. Position 5: 1 ≠ 0. Position 6: 0 = 0. Position 7: 1 = 1.
  4. Two positions differ, so the distance is 2.

Answer: Option (B) — 2.

Common misconception. The slip is to compare the decimal values or to count matching positions instead of differing ones.

Takeaway. Distance = number of differing positions = weight of the XOR of the two words: 1011101 ⊕ 1001001 = 0010100, which has weight 2.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A block code has minimum Hamming distance 5. How many bit errors can it (i) detect and (ii) correct?
questions.question_html:
Question 21MCQmediumerror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingstandard textbookMarks: 1

A block code has minimum Hamming distance 5. How many bit errors can it (i) detect and (ii) correct?
options: Detect 4, correct 2
Detect 2, correct 4
Detect 5, correct 2
Detect 2, correct 1
options_html: ADetect 4, correct 2
BDetect 2, correct 4
CDetect 5, correct 2
DDetect 2, correct 1
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With minimum distance d: detection capability is d − 1 errors, correction capability is ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋ errors.

Step by step.

  1. d = 5, so up to d − 1 = 4 errors can be detected.
  2. Correction: ⌊4/2⌋ = 2 errors.
  3. Intuition: a received word with 2 errors is still strictly nearer its own codeword than any other (distance 2 against at least 3).

Answer: Option (A) — detect 4, correct 2.

Common misconception. Candidates often answer ‘detect 5’. With 5 errors a word can land exactly on another codeword, so 5 errors are not detectable.

Takeaway. Memorise the pair: detect ≤ d−1, correct ≤ ⌊(d−1)/2⌋. Every error-detection question reduces to these two.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A single-error-correcting Hamming code is to be built for 16 data bits. What is the minimum number of parity bits required?
questions.question_html:
Question 22NATmediumerror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A single-error-correcting Hamming code is to be built for 16 data bits.
What is the minimum number of parity bits required?

Answer format: an integer number of parity bits.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With m data bits and r parity bits, the r check positions must be able to address every one of the m + r positions plus the ‘no error’ case: m + r + 1 ≤ 2r.

Step by step.

  1. Try r = 4: 16 + 4 + 1 = 21 > 16 = 2⁴, so 4 parity bits cannot address all error patterns.
  2. Try r = 5: 16 + 5 + 1 = 22 ≤ 32 = 2⁵, which works.
  3. So the minimum is 5 parity bits, giving a 21-bit codeword.

Answer: 5 parity bits.

Common misconception. The common error is to use 2r ≥ m only, which gives 4. The parity bits also occupy positions that must be addressable, and the all-zero syndrome must be reserved for ‘no error’.

Takeaway. For Hamming codes, solve the smallest r with m + r + 1 ≤ 2r. For m = 4, 7, 8, 16 the answers are 3, 4, 4, 5.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about CRC and checksums are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 23MSQharderror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about CRC and checksums are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A CRC whose generator polynomial has at least two non-zero terms detects every single-bit error.
A CRC with a generator polynomial of degree r detects every burst error of length at most r.
If the CRC remainder is zero, the received frame is guaranteed to be error-free.
CRC arithmetic is polynomial division over GF(2), where addition and subtraction are both the XOR operation.
options_html: AA CRC whose generator polynomial has at least two non-zero terms detects every single-bit error.
BA CRC with a generator polynomial of degree r detects every burst error of length at most r.
CIf the CRC remainder is zero, the received frame is guaranteed to be error-free.
DCRC arithmetic is polynomial division over GF(2), where addition and subtraction are both the XOR operation.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. CRC treats the frame as a polynomial over GF(2); the properties follow from divisibility by the generator polynomial g(x).

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — a single-bit error is xi, and g(x) with two or more terms cannot divide a monomial.
  2. (B) True — a burst of length ≤ r has degree below r, so it cannot be a non-zero multiple of g(x).
  3. (C) False — a zero remainder only means the received polynomial is divisible by g(x); an error pattern that is itself a multiple of g(x) escapes detection.
  4. (D) True — coefficients are in GF(2), so +1 = −1 and both operations are XOR.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Statement (C) is the classic over-claim. CRC is a detection scheme with a small, bounded probability of a missed error, not a guarantee — which is exactly why (D)'s algebraic view matters.

Takeaway. Learn the two guarantees (all single-bit errors; all bursts of length ≤ r) and the one non-guarantee (no error-free certification).

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A datagram header is to be protected by the 16-bit Internet checksum. The three 16-bit words to be summed are 0x1234, 0x5678 and 0x9ABC. Using one's complement arithmetic, what is the checksum field value?
questions.question_html:
Question 24MCQharderror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A datagram header is to be protected by the 16-bit Internet checksum. The three 16-bit words to be summed are 0x1234, 0x5678 and 0x9ABC. Using one's complement arithmetic, what is the checksum field value?
options: 0xFC96
0xFC95
0xFC69
options_html: A0x0369
B0xFC96
C0xFC95
D0xFC69
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The Internet checksum adds the 16-bit words in one's complement arithmetic (end-around carry), then takes the one's complement of the result.

Step by step.

  1. 0x1234 + 0x5678 = 0x68AC.
  2. 0x68AC + 0x9ABC = 0x10368, which overflows 16 bits.
  3. End-around carry: 0x0368 + 1 = 0x0369.
  4. Checksum = one's complement of 0x0369 = 0xFFFF − 0x0369 = 0xFC96.

Answer: Option (B) — 0xFC96.

Common misconception. Dropping the end-around carry gives 0xFC95, and forgetting the complement gives 0x0369; both are offered as options. Note that 0xFC96 is not the arithmetic negation in two's complement either.

Takeaway. Checksum routine: sum with wraparound, fold the carry in, then complement. Verify by adding the checksum back — the total must be 0xFFFF.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A CRC is computed with the generator polynomial x³ + 1, whose bit pattern is 1001. The message bits are 1101 and three zeros are appended before division. Enter the decimal value of the resulting 3-bit remainder.
questions.question_html:
Question 25NATmediumerror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A CRC is computed with the generator polynomial x³ + 1, whose bit pattern is 1001. The message bits are 1101 and three zeros are appended before division.
Enter the decimal value of the resulting 3-bit remainder.

Answer format: an integer, the decimal value of the 3-bit remainder.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. CRC division is long division over GF(2): align the divisor under the leading 1 of the current remainder and XOR, with no borrows or carries.

Step by step.

  1. Append three zeros: 1101000.
  2. Leading 4 bits 1101 ⊕ 1001 = 0100; bring down 0 → 1000; 1000 ⊕ 1001 = 0001.
  3. Bring down the next 0 → 0010; the leading bit is 0, so XOR nothing. Bring down the last 0 → 0100; again nothing.
  4. The 3-bit remainder is 100, i.e. 4 in decimal.

Answer: 4 (remainder 100).

Common misconception. The trap is ordinary binary subtraction with borrows. In GF(2) there is no borrow: XOR is the only operation, so a step where the leading bit is 0 just shifts down the next bit.

Takeaway. For a degree-r generator the remainder is always r bits; read it as a plain binary number if the answer must be decimal.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which OSI layer is responsible for data compression and for converting between different data representations such as ASCII and EBCDIC?
questions.question_html:
Question 1MCQeasyosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which OSI layer is responsible for data compression and for converting between different data representations such as ASCII and EBCDIC?
options: Session layer
Application layer
Data link layer
Presentation layer
options_html: Session layer
Application layer
Data link layer
Presentation layer
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The OSI model separates user-facing work from syntax work. The application layer offers the service the user asks for, the presentation layer fixes the form of the data (compression, encryption, character-set conversion), and the session layer manages the dialogue between two applications.

Step by step.

  1. Compression removes redundancy from a representation; it changes how the data is encoded, not what service is requested.
  2. Code conversion between ASCII and EBCDIC is the same kind of job: it rewrites the syntax of the data.
  3. Both are exactly the functions the presentation layer owns.
  4. The session layer manages dialogue control (checkpoints, synchronisation) and the application layer handles the user service itself.

Answer: Option (D) — the presentation layer.

Common misconception. Encryption and compression are often attributed to the application layer because an application often requests them. In the OSI reference model they belong to presentation, which is exactly the layer the TCP/IP model does not have.

Takeaway. Ask what is being changed: the service (application), the form of the data (presentation), or the dialogue (session).

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The protocol data units (PDUs) of the transport, network and data link layers are, in that order, called:
questions.question_html:
Question 2MCQeasyosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

The protocol data units (PDUs) of the transport, network and data link layers are, in that order, called:
options: frame, packet, segment
segment, datagram, frame
datagram, segment, frame
segment, frame, datagram
options_html: frame, packet, segment
segment, datagram, frame
datagram, segment, frame
segment, frame, datagram
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each layer names the unit it hands down: the transport layer produces a segment, the network layer a datagram (packet), and the data link layer a frame; the physical layer moves raw bits.

Step by step.

  1. The transport layer takes the byte stream and adds its header, producing a segment.
  2. The network layer wraps the segment in an IP header, producing a packet or datagram.
  3. The data link layer wraps the datagram with a header and a trailer, producing a frame.
  4. So the order transport → network → data link gives segment → datagram → frame.

Answer: Option (B) — segment, datagram, frame.

Common misconception. The pairs are easy to rotate. The trap is placing the frame before the packet; a frame is the outermost encapsulation, so it is produced last on the way down and removed first on the way up.

Takeaway. Anchor the order by encapsulation depth: segment inside datagram inside frame.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Flow control and error control appear at more than one layer. Which statement is correct?
questions.question_html:
Question 3MCQmediumosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsstandard textbookMarks: 1

Flow control and error control appear at more than one layer. Which statement is correct?
options: The data link layer controls flow and errors between two adjacent nodes on one link, while the transport layer controls them between the two end processes.
Only the transport layer performs flow control; the data link layer has none.
The network layer performs end-to-end flow control between processes.
Flow control in the data link layer protects against errors introduced inside routers.
options_html: The data link layer controls flow and errors between two adjacent nodes on one link, while the transport layer controls them between the two end processes.
Only the transport layer performs flow control; the data link layer has none.
The network layer performs end-to-end flow control between processes.
Flow control in the data link layer protects against errors introduced inside routers.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. OSI draws a scope line: the data link layer works link by link between adjacent nodes, the transport layer works end to end between processes. Both perform flow and error control, but over different spans.

Step by step.

  1. A frame exists only on one link, so its acknowledgement and window can only concern that link — that is link-by-link control.
  2. A segment survives every hop, so its window and acknowledgement concern the two end processes — that is end-to-end control.
  3. The network layer forwards packets; it does not run a window between processes.
  4. Errors introduced inside a router are exactly what the end-to-end transport checksum is there to catch, not the link-layer window.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Candidates read ‘flow control’ as a single function belonging to one layer. It is a family of mechanisms, and the same name at two layers means two different scopes.

Takeaway. Name the scope before naming the layer: adjacent nodes → data link, end processes → transport.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A router forwards an IPv4 packet that arrives on one Ethernet and leaves on another. Ignoring NAT, which of the following are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 4MSQmediumosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A router forwards an IPv4 packet that arrives on one Ethernet and leaves on another. Ignoring NAT, which of the following are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The source and destination MAC addresses of the outgoing frame differ from those of the incoming frame.
The source and destination IPv4 addresses in the packet are unchanged.
The TTL field is decremented by one.
The transport-layer checksum must be recomputed by the router because the frame addresses changed.
options_html: The source and destination MAC addresses of the outgoing frame differ from those of the incoming frame.
The source and destination IPv4 addresses in the packet are unchanged.
The TTL field is decremented by one.
The transport-layer checksum must be recomputed by the router because the frame addresses changed.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A router terminates the link layer on each interface and forwards at the network layer, so link-layer addresses are local to a link while network-layer addresses are end to end.

Step by step.

  1. MAC addresses identify a network card on one link. The outgoing frame is built for the next hop, so both MAC addresses are rewritten.
  2. The IPv4 addresses name the end hosts and are carried unchanged through every router (NAT aside).
  3. The TTL is decremented at each router so that packets cannot loop forever.
  4. The transport checksum covers a pseudo-header of IP addresses and the transport payload; neither changes here, so the router does not recompute it.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. ‘The router changes the addresses, so it must fix the checksum’ conflates the two address spaces. Only the MAC addresses change, and no transport checksum covers them.

Takeaway. Per hop: MAC addresses and TTL change. End to end: IP addresses and the transport checksum survive.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A router forwards IPv4 packets between its attached links. It implements the physical and data link layers on each link and the network layer for forwarding; it runs no transport-layer or application-layer protocol of its own. How many of the seven OSI layers does this router implement?
questions.question_html:
Question 5NATeasyosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A router forwards IPv4 packets between its attached links. It implements the physical and data link layers on each link and the network layer for forwarding; it runs no transport-layer or application-layer protocol of its own.
How many of the seven OSI layers does this router implement?

Answer format: an integer from 1 to 7.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The number of OSI layers a device implements is the number of distinct layers whose functions it actually performs, not the number of headers it happens to read.

Step by step.

  1. Physical layer: it drives the line and moves bits on each interface.
  2. Data link layer: it frames and unframes, checks the frame check sequence and addresses the next hop.
  3. Network layer: it runs the routing table and forwards the packet.
  4. It runs no transport or application protocol, and OSI session and presentation functions are absent entirely, so the count stops at three.

Answer: 3 layers.

Common misconception. Counting all seven because the router ‘sees’ the whole packet. Reading a header is not implementing a layer; the router never processes the transport header at all.

Takeaway. Count the layers whose functions the device performs, and stop where its processing stops.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Every link uses a frame check sequence that each router verifies and recomputes. Why does TCP nevertheless carry its own checksum?
questions.question_html:
Question 6MCQhardosi-and-tcp-ip-modelsoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Every link uses a frame check sequence that each router verifies and recomputes. Why does TCP nevertheless carry its own checksum?
options: Because a frame check sequence cannot detect burst errors.

Because a packet can be corrupted inside a router, after its incoming frame check sequence has been verified, and the outgoing link will then protect the corrupted packet with a fresh, valid frame check sequence.
Because the frame check sequence covers only the frame header.
Because routers strip the frame check sequence before forwarding the frame.
options_html: Because a frame check sequence cannot detect burst errors.

Because a packet can be corrupted inside a router, after its incoming frame check sequence has been verified, and the outgoing link will then protect the corrupted packet with a fresh, valid frame check sequence.
Because the frame check sequence covers only the frame header.
Because routers strip the frame check sequence before forwarding the frame.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A hop-by-hop check protects a hop; it cannot protect the path. The end-to-end argument places a correctness check at the endpoints precisely because intermediate systems can introduce errors of their own.

Step by step.

  1. The incoming frame check sequence is verified when the frame arrives, so it says nothing about anything that happens afterwards.
  2. Inside a router the packet is held in memory, moved across a switching fabric and rewritten; any of these can corrupt it.
  3. The outgoing frame gets a newly computed check sequence over the corrupted bits, which therefore validates perfectly at the next hop.
  4. Only a check computed at the source and verified at the destination spans the whole path, which is what the TCP checksum provides.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. The tempting answer is that the link check is somehow weak. It is strong; it is simply local. A correct hop check on a packet corrupted inside a router is a false reassurance, and that gap is exactly what the transport checksum closes.

Takeaway. A check protects the span over which it is computed and verified; hop-by-hop protection leaves the router itself uncovered.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which component of nodal delay grows without bound as the traffic intensity La/R approaches 1?
questions.question_html:
Question 7MCQeasytransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which component of nodal delay grows without bound as the traffic intensity La/R approaches 1?
options: Transmission delay
Propagation delay
Queueing delay
Processing delay
options_html: Transmission delay
Propagation delay
Queueing delay
Processing delay
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Nodal delay is the sum of processing, queueing, transmission and propagation delay. Only queueing delay depends on how busy the link is.

Step by step.

  1. Transmission delay is L/R, fixed by packet size and link rate.
  2. Propagation delay is d/s, fixed by distance and signal speed.
  3. Processing delay is a small fixed cost per packet.
  4. Queueing delay is the time a packet waits behind others; as the arrival rate approaches the service rate the backlog, and hence the wait, diverges.

Answer: Option (C) — queueing delay.

Common misconception. Reading La/R as a transmission-delay formula. The product La is the bit arrival rate and R the bit service rate, so the ratio measures load, not transmission time.

Takeaway. Only queueing delay is a function of traffic; the other three are properties of the packet, the link and the distance.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Packets of 1500 bytes arrive at a link of rate 1 Mbps at an average rate of 60 packets per second. What is the traffic intensity La/R?
questions.question_html:
Question 8MCQmediumtransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Packets of 1500 bytes arrive at a link of rate 1 Mbps at an average rate of 60 packets per second. What is the traffic intensity La/R?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Traffic intensity is the ratio of the bit arrival rate La to the bit service rate R; below 1 the queue is stable, above 1 it grows without bound.

Step by step.

  1. Packet size L = 1500 bytes = 1500 × 8 = 12000 bits.
  2. Arrival rate a = 60 packets per second, so the bit arrival rate is 60 × 12000 = 720000 bits/s.
  3. Link rate R = 1 Mbps = 1000000 bits/s.
  4. Traffic intensity = 720000 / 1000000 = 0.72.

Answer: 0.72 — option (A).

Common misconception. Using 1500 instead of 12000, which mixes bytes with bits and gives 0.072. The link rate is in bits per second, so the packet size must be converted to bits first.

Takeaway. Convert to bits once, at the start, and the ratio is dimensionless.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A link has a bandwidth of 10 Mbps and a one-way propagation delay of 25 ms. A sender keeps the link fully utilised with a sliding window. Ignoring header overhead and acknowledgements, what is the minimum window size in bits?
questions.question_html:
Question 9NATmediumtransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A link has a bandwidth of 10 Mbps and a one-way propagation delay of 25 ms. A sender keeps the link fully utilised with a sliding window. Ignoring header overhead and acknowledgements, what is the minimum window size in bits?

Answer format: an integer number of bits.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A sender can have at most one bandwidth-delay product of data in flight; the window must be at least that large to keep the pipe full.

Step by step.

  1. The bandwidth-delay product is R × dprop.
  2. R = 10 Mbps = 107 bits/s.
  3. dprop = 25 ms = 0.025 s.
  4. Window = 107 × 0.025 = 250000 bits.

Answer: 250000 bits.

Common misconception. Using the round-trip time. The window must cover the bits that can be in the pipe in one direction; doubling to the RTT overstates the requirement by a factor of two.

Takeaway. Window for full utilisation = bandwidth × one-way propagation delay, in matching units.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: N packets, each of L bits, are sent back to back from a source to a destination over a path of k store-and-forward links, each of bandwidth R. Propagation, processing and queueing delays are negligible. What is the time from the instant the first bit leaves the source until the last bit reaches the destination?
questions.question_html:
Question 10MCQhardtransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

N packets, each of L bits, are sent back to back from a source to a destination over a path of k store-and-forward links, each of bandwidth R. Propagation, processing and queueing delays are negligible. What is the time from the instant the first bit leaves the source until the last bit reaches the destination?
options: (k + N)L/R
(k + N − 1)L/R
kNL/R
(k + N − 1)R/L
options_html: (k + N)L/R
(k + N − 1)L/R
kNL/R
(k + N − 1)R/L
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With store-and-forward, the first packet pays one transmission delay on every link; each of the remaining N − 1 packets then emerges one transmission delay after the previous one.

Step by step.

  1. The first packet must be fully received and retransmitted at each of the k links: time kL/R.
  2. After that the pipeline is full, and every further packet appears at the destination L/R later.
  3. There are N − 1 further packets, contributing (N − 1)L/R.
  4. Total = kL/R + (N − 1)L/R = (k + N − 1)L/R.

Answer: Option (B) — (k + N − 1)L/R.

Common misconception. Multiplying to get kNL/R treats the links as serial rather than pipelined, which is what a store-and-forward chain does not do once packets are flowing. Option (A) forgets that the last packet needs no extra link time after it has traversed all k links.

Takeaway. Count the first packet's full traversal, then add one transmission delay per remaining packet.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about delay and throughput are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 11MSQmediumtransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about delay and throughput are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The throughput of an end-to-end path cannot exceed the bandwidth of its bottleneck link.
Propagation delay increases with the size of the packet.
For a fixed packet size and arrival rate, increasing the link bandwidth reduces the traffic intensity.
In the ideal queueing model, once the traffic intensity exceeds 1 the queue at a store-and-forward router grows without bound.
options_html: The throughput of an end-to-end path cannot exceed the bandwidth of its bottleneck link.
Propagation delay increases with the size of the packet.
For a fixed packet size and arrival rate, increasing the link bandwidth reduces the traffic intensity.
In the ideal queueing model, once the traffic intensity exceeds 1 the queue at a store-and-forward router grows without bound.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Throughput is set by the slowest link on the path; traffic intensity is La/R, so raising R lowers it; and a queue is stable only while the arrival rate stays below the service rate.

Step by step.

  1. The bottleneck link must carry every bit of the flow, so it caps the end-to-end rate: (A) is true.
  2. Propagation delay is d/s, a property of distance and signal speed; it does not see the packet at all: (B) is false.
  3. La/R falls as R rises with L and a fixed: (C) is true.
  4. With arrival rate above service rate the backlog increases by a positive amount per unit time, so the queue length diverges: (D) is true.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (B) is the standard error: a longer packet spends longer on the wire, which is transmission delay, not propagation delay. The bit at the head of the packet still crosses the link in d/s seconds.

Takeaway. Transmission delay belongs to the packet and the rate; propagation delay belongs to the wire.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A 500-byte packet is sent over a 1 Mbps link that is 1000 km long; the signal propagates at 2 × 108 m/s. Ignoring queueing and processing, what is the one-way delay?
questions.question_html:
Question 12MCQeasytransmission-delays-bandwidth-delay-productoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A 500-byte packet is sent over a 1 Mbps link that is 1000 km long; the signal propagates at 2 × 108 m/s. Ignoring queueing and processing, what is the one-way delay?
options: 4 ms
5 ms
9 ms
20 ms
options_html: 4 ms
5 ms
9 ms
20 ms
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. One-way delay is the sum of transmission delay L/R and propagation delay d/s.

Step by step.

  1. L = 500 bytes = 4000 bits, so transmission delay = 4000 / 106 = 4 ms.
  2. d = 1000 km = 106 m, so propagation delay = 106 / (2 × 108) = 5 ms.
  3. The two are independent and additive: 4 + 5 = 9 ms.
  4. Neither queueing nor processing delay is present, so nothing else is added.

Answer: 9 ms — option (C).

Common misconception. Reporting 4 ms or 5 ms, one component only. The other classic slip is subtracting instead of adding because the two delays feel like alternatives; they occur one after the other on a single link.

Takeaway. Put the packet on the wire (L/R), then let the last bit travel (d/s): add the two.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: In character-count framing, the count field of a frame states:
questions.question_html:
Question 13MCQeasyframing-bit-byte-stuffingstandard textbookMarks: 1

In character-count framing, the count field of a frame states:
options: the number of characters in the data field only
the number of frames that follow it in the stream
the number of bits in the frame
the number of characters in the whole frame, including the count field itself
options_html: the number of characters in the data field only
the number of frames that follow it in the stream
the number of bits in the frame
the number of characters in the whole frame, including the count field itself
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Character-count framing prefixes each frame with a field giving the length of that frame in characters, counted from the count field itself to the end of the frame.

Step by step.

  1. The receiver reads the count field first and then consumes exactly that many characters to reach the end of the frame.
  2. The count must therefore include the count field, or the receiver would stop short by the width of that field.
  3. It is a character count, not a bit count, and it describes this frame only.
  4. Everything after those characters is the start of the next frame.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Reading the count as the payload length. If it excluded the header the receiver would lose synchronisation after the very first frame, which is the same failure mode as a corrupted count.

Takeaway. The count spans the frame it heads, count field included.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A data stream of 1024 bits is transmitted with bit stuffing, where a 0 is inserted after every five consecutive 1s. What is the largest number of bits that can be inserted for this stream?
questions.question_html:
Question 14NATeasyframing-bit-byte-stuffingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A data stream of 1024 bits is transmitted with bit stuffing, where a 0 is inserted after every five consecutive 1s.
What is the largest number of bits that can be inserted for this stream?

Answer format: an integer number of inserted bits.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Bit stuffing inserts one 0 for every completed run of five 1s; the number inserted is therefore maximised when the data is all 1s.

Step by step.

  1. Take the worst case: all 1024 data bits are 1.
  2. Insertions happen after bits 5, 10, 15, …, that is after every multiple of 5.
  3. The number of multiples of 5 not exceeding 1024 is ⌊1024 / 5⌋ = 204.
  4. The remaining 1024 − 5 × 204 = 4 trailing 1s do not complete another run of five, so nothing further is inserted.

Answer: 204 inserted bits.

Common misconception. Rounding up to 205. The final partial run of four 1s never reaches five, so no sixth insertion can occur; a stuffed stream grows by at most one bit per five data bits, never more.

Takeaway. Worst case for bit stuffing is an all-ones stream, and the count is ⌊n/5⌋.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The bit stream 0111110011111001 is received inside a bit-oriented frame, where the sender inserted a 0 after every five consecutive 1s. After de-stuffing, what is the original data?
questions.question_html:
Question 15MCQmediumframing-bit-byte-stuffingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

The bit stream 0111110011111001 is received inside a bit-oriented frame, where the sender inserted a 0 after every five consecutive 1s. After de-stuffing, what is the original data?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The receiver scans left to right, counts consecutive 1s, and deletes the 0 that immediately follows the fifth 1; the counter then restarts.

Step by step.

  1. Read 0: no run yet. Then 11111 completes a run of five 1s.
  2. The next bit is 0 and is the stuffed bit, so it is deleted; the counter restarts at 0.
  3. The next bit is 0, which is genuine data; the counter stays at 0.
  4. Then 11111 completes another run of five, and the following 0 is deleted.
  5. The last two bits 0 and 1 are genuine, giving 01111101111101.

Answer: Option (A) — 01111101111101.

Common misconception. Deleting every 0 that follows a run of 1s, including the genuine data 0. Exactly one 0 is removed per completed run of five 1s, and the run counter resets after each removal.

Takeaway. De-stuffing is deterministic: one deletion per run of five 1s, then restart the count.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about framing are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 16MSQeasyframing-bit-byte-stuffingstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about framing are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Byte stuffing works on arbitrary binary data only if the escape byte itself is escaped.
Bit stuffing changes the length of a frame by at most one bit.
In HDLC a receiver that sees seven consecutive 1s treats the frame as aborted.
Bit stuffing guarantees that the flag pattern never occurs inside the frame body.
options_html: Byte stuffing works on arbitrary binary data only if the escape byte itself is escaped.
Bit stuffing changes the length of a frame by at most one bit.
In HDLC a receiver that sees seven consecutive 1s treats the frame as aborted.
Bit stuffing guarantees that the flag pattern never occurs inside the frame body.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Stuffing exists to keep the flag pattern out of the data. In byte-oriented framing the escape byte is data too, so it must escape itself; in bit-oriented framing the flag contains six consecutive 1s, which stuffing makes unreachable inside the body.

Step by step.

  1. If the escape byte were not itself escaped, a data escape byte would be read as the start of an escape sequence: (A) is true.
  2. A long frame of all 1s gains one bit per five, so the growth is proportional to the frame, not bounded by one bit: (B) is false.
  3. HDLC reserves seven consecutive 1s as the abort sequence, which stuffing can never produce in valid data: (C) is true.
  4. Stuffing removes any run of six 1s, and the flag 01111110 contains six, so it cannot appear in the body: (D) is true.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (B) confuses ‘one bit per insertion’ with ‘one bit per frame’. The number of insertions scales with the length of the data.

Takeaway. Byte stuffing must escape the flag and the escape; bit stuffing must break any run of six 1s.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the robustness and overhead of the three framing methods are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 17MSQhardframing-bit-byte-stuffingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about the robustness and overhead of the three framing methods are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: In the worst case, byte stuffing can more than double the length of the frame body.
A single corrupted count field in character-count framing destroys the framing of every following frame in the stream.
Flag-based framing is self-synchronising: after an error the receiver can recover at the next flag.
The overhead of bit stuffing is at most one extra bit for every five data bits.
options_html: In the worst case, byte stuffing can more than double the length of the frame body.
A single corrupted count field in character-count framing destroys the framing of every following frame in the stream.
Flag-based framing is self-synchronising: after an error the receiver can recover at the next flag.
The overhead of bit stuffing is at most one extra bit for every five data bits.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The three methods trade overhead against recoverability. A count field is compact but has no redundancy, so one error desynchronises the stream; flags cost more but let the receiver resynchronise.

Step by step.

  1. Byte stuffing inserts exactly one escape byte before each flag or escape byte, so the body at most doubles: (A) is false.
  2. The count field is the only thing that tells the receiver where the frame ends; if it is wrong, every later frame boundary is wrong too: (B) is true.
  3. A receiver that loses its place scans for the next flag pattern and resumes there: (C) is true.
  4. Stuffing inserts one bit per completed run of five 1s, so overhead never exceeds one bit in six: (D) is true.

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (A) feels plausible because escaping every byte doubles the size, but each escaped byte becomes exactly two bytes — never three — so doubling is the exact worst case, not an underestimate of it.

Takeaway. Character count is cheapest and most fragile; flags cost more and recover themselves.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A frame carries 300 bytes of data, of which 12 bytes are 0x7E and 5 bytes are 0x7D. Byte stuffing inserts ESC = 0x7D before each such byte. How many bytes are transmitted between the opening and closing flags?
questions.question_html:
Question 18MCQmediumframing-bit-byte-stuffingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A frame carries 300 bytes of data, of which 12 bytes are 0x7E and 5 bytes are 0x7D. Byte stuffing inserts ESC = 0x7D before each such byte. How many bytes are transmitted between the opening and closing flags?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Byte stuffing leaves ordinary bytes alone and turns each flag or escape byte into a two-byte sequence, so the body grows by exactly the number of such bytes.

Step by step.

  1. The 12 bytes equal to 0x7E each become two bytes: 12 extra bytes.
  2. The 5 bytes equal to 0x7D are escaped as well, since the escape byte must escape itself: 5 extra bytes.
  3. The other 300 − 12 − 5 = 283 bytes are transmitted unchanged.
  4. Total between the flags = 283 + 12 × 2 + 5 × 2 = 283 + 24 + 10 = 317 bytes.

Answer: 317 bytes — option (D).

Common misconception. Forgetting that 0x7D is the escape byte and so must be escaped itself, which gives 312. Counting the opening and closing flags inside the figure is the other slip; they are asked for separately.

Takeaway. Escaped bytes double, and the escape byte is one of them.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following schemes can correct a single-bit error?
questions.question_html:
Question 19MCQeasyerror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which of the following schemes can correct a single-bit error?
options: A single parity bit per block
A block code with minimum Hamming distance 2
A Hamming code with minimum distance 3
A 16-bit Internet checksum
options_html: A single parity bit per block
A block code with minimum Hamming distance 2
A Hamming code with minimum distance 3
A 16-bit Internet checksum
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Correction needs the received word to be nearer one codeword than any other, which requires minimum distance at least 3; distance 2 only guarantees detection.

Step by step.

  1. A code with minimum distance d corrects ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋ errors.
  2. A single parity bit gives d = 2, so it corrects 0 errors.
  3. A code with d = 2 also corrects 0 errors — it detects single errors only.
  4. A checksum is an arithmetic check with no distance guarantee, so it cannot locate an error at all.
  5. A Hamming code with d = 3 corrects ⌊2/2⌋ = 1 error.

Answer: Option (C) — a Hamming code with minimum distance 3.

Common misconception. Expecting a parity bit to point at the bad bit. Parity tells you that something is wrong; locating it needs several overlapping parity groups, which is exactly what a Hamming code builds.

Takeaway. Detect needs d ≥ e + 1; correct needs d ≥ 2t + 1.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A single parity bit is appended to a block of data. Which error pattern is guaranteed to be detected?
questions.question_html:
Question 20MCQeasyerror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A single parity bit is appended to a block of data. Which error pattern is guaranteed to be detected?
options: Any single-bit error
Any two-bit error
Any odd number of bit errors
Any burst of three consecutive bit errors
options_html: Any single-bit error
Any two-bit error
Any odd number of bit errors
Any burst of three consecutive bit errors
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A single parity bit records the parity of the block, so it detects exactly those error patterns that change the parity, that is, patterns of odd weight.

Step by step.

  1. The parity bit is chosen so that the total number of 1s has a fixed parity.
  2. Flipping one bit changes that parity, so any single-bit error is detected — but that is a special case, not the general guarantee.
  3. Flipping two bits leaves the parity unchanged, so a two-bit error is undetected.
  4. Flipping any odd number of bits changes the parity, so every odd-weight pattern is detected.
  5. A burst of three flips the parity too, but a burst of two does not, so the burst statement is not a guarantee.

Answer: Option (C) — any odd number of bit errors.

Common misconception. Believing parity detects all single-bit errors and therefore all small errors. Parity is blind to every even-weight pattern, including the very common two-bit error.

Takeaway. Single parity detects odd weight, nothing else.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A CRC uses the generator polynomial x3 + x + 1, whose bit pattern is 1011. The message bits are 1100 and three zeros are appended before division. Enter the decimal value of the resulting 3-bit remainder.
questions.question_html:
Question 21NATmediumerror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A CRC uses the generator polynomial x3 + x + 1, whose bit pattern is 1011. The message bits are 1100 and three zeros are appended before division.
Enter the decimal value of the resulting 3-bit remainder.

Answer format: an integer, the decimal value of the 3-bit remainder.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. CRC is polynomial division over GF(2): subtraction is XOR, the message is shifted left by the degree of the generator, and the remainder is the check bits.

Step by step.

  1. Degree of the generator is 3, so append three zeros: 1100000.
  2. XOR 1100000 with 1011 aligned at the left: 1100 ⊕ 1011 = 0111, giving 0111000.
  3. Bring the leading 1 into position and XOR again: 1110 ⊕ 1011 = 0101, leaving 010100.
  4. Once more: 1010 ⊕ 1011 = 0001, leaving 00010.
  5. No further leading 1 remains, so the 3-bit remainder is 010 = 2 in decimal.

Answer: 2 (remainder 010).

Common misconception. Subtracting in ordinary integer arithmetic. Over GF(2) there is no borrow: 1100 ⊕ 1011 = 0111, not 0001. The other slip is appending two zeros instead of three, which silently changes the remainder.

Takeaway. Append as many zeros as the generator's degree, then XOR-shift; never subtract.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A CRC generator polynomial has degree r. Which class of burst errors is it guaranteed to detect?
questions.question_html:
Question 22MCQmediumerror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingstandard textbookMarks: 1

A CRC generator polynomial has degree r. Which class of burst errors is it guaranteed to detect?
options: Every burst error of length at most r
Every burst error of length at most r + 1
Every burst error of length exactly r + 1
Every burst error, whatever its length
options_html: Every burst error of length at most r
Every burst error of length at most r + 1
Every burst error of length exactly r + 1
Every burst error, whatever its length
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A degree-r generator has a non-zero constant term, so any error polynomial of degree below r cannot be a multiple of it; that is the burst guarantee.

Step by step.

  1. A burst of length k is an error polynomial of the form xi(1 + … + xk−1).
  2. The generator G(x) of degree r divides such a polynomial only if it divides the bracket, which has degree k − 1.
  3. When k ≤ r the bracket has degree below r, so it cannot be a non-zero multiple of G(x) and the error is always detected.
  4. Bursts longer than r can slip through, so the guarantee stops exactly at r.

Answer: Option (A) — every burst of length at most r.

Common misconception. Extending the guarantee to r + 1 or claiming CRC detects everything. A CRC detects all single-bit errors, all odd numbers of errors when G has (x + 1) as a factor, and all bursts up to length r — and nothing more in general.

Takeaway. Degree r buys burst protection up to length r, full stop.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about error-detecting and error-correcting codes are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 23MSQmediumerror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about error-detecting and error-correcting codes are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The Internet checksum adds the 16-bit words using two's complement arithmetic.
A code with minimum Hamming distance d detects any pattern of at most d − 1 bit errors.
A code with minimum Hamming distance d corrects any pattern of at most ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋ bit errors.
Adding one parity bit to a block raises the minimum distance of the code from 1 to 2.
options_html: The Internet checksum adds the 16-bit words using two's complement arithmetic.
A code with minimum Hamming distance d detects any pattern of at most d − 1 bit errors.
A code with minimum Hamming distance d corrects any pattern of at most ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋ bit errors.
Adding one parity bit to a block raises the minimum distance of the code from 1 to 2.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Minimum distance fixes both guarantees: detection up to d − 1, correction up to ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋. The Internet checksum is one's complement, not two's complement.

Step by step.

  1. Two codewords at distance d cannot be joined by an error of weight below d, so any such error lands off the code: (B) is true.
  2. Correcting t errors needs disjoint balls of radius t, which requires d ≥ 2t + 1, hence t = ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋: (C) is true.
  3. Without a parity bit any word is a codeword, so d = 1; one parity bit makes every pair differ in at least two places: (D) is true.
  4. The Internet checksum uses one's complement arithmetic with end-around carry: (A) is false.

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (A) is a favourite trap because two's complement is the arithmetic most programmers reach for. The Internet checksum predates that habit: it is one's complement, which is why the end-around carry exists and why there are two representations of zero.

Takeaway. Distance drives the guarantees; the Internet checksum is one's complement with end-around carry.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A block code has minimum Hamming distance 6. Which of the following states the largest guaranteed detection and correction capability?
questions.question_html:
Question 24MCQharderror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A block code has minimum Hamming distance 6. Which of the following states the largest guaranteed detection and correction capability?
options: Detect up to 5 bit errors, correct up to 2
Detect up to 5 bit errors, correct up to 3
Detect up to 6 bit errors, correct up to 2
Detect up to 6 bit errors, correct up to 3
options_html: Detect up to 5 bit errors, correct up to 2
Detect up to 5 bit errors, correct up to 3
Detect up to 6 bit errors, correct up to 2
Detect up to 6 bit errors, correct up to 3
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Detection is guaranteed up to d − 1 and correction up to ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋; with d = 6 these are 5 and 2.

Step by step.

  1. d − 1 = 5, so every pattern of weight at most 5 is detected.
  2. ⌊(6 − 1)/2⌋ = ⌊2.5⌋ = 2, so up to 2 errors can be corrected.
  3. Correcting 3 errors would need d ≥ 2 × 3 + 1 = 7, which this code does not have.
  4. Detecting 6 errors would need d ≥ 7, and a weight-6 error can land exactly on another codeword at distance 6.

Answer: Option (A) — detect 5, correct 2.

Common misconception. Rounding (d − 1)/2 up, or assuming detection and correction capacities can both be pushed to the maximum at once. The two guarantees are separate budgets taken from the same distance.

Takeaway. With d = 6: detect 5, correct 2 — the floor, never the ceiling.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A single-error-correcting Hamming code uses r = 6 parity bits. What is the largest number of data bits it can protect?
questions.question_html:
Question 25NATharderror-detection-crc-checksum-hammingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A single-error-correcting Hamming code uses r = 6 parity bits.
What is the largest number of data bits it can protect?

Answer format: an integer number of data bits.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With r parity bits the syndrome has 2r values: one for ‘no error’ and one for each of the m + r single-bit positions. Hence m + r + 1 ≤ 2r.

Step by step.

  1. Write the Hamming condition: m + r + 1 ≤ 2r.
  2. Substitute r = 6: 26 = 64, so m + 6 + 1 ≤ 64.
  3. Therefore m ≤ 64 − 7 = 57.
  4. With m = 57 the code has 57 + 6 = 63 bit positions, and the 64th syndrome value is reserved for ‘no error’.

Answer: 57 data bits.

Common misconception. Using 2r ≥ m + r and answering 58, which forgets the all-zero syndrome that must mean ‘no error’. The +1 in the inequality is that reserved pattern.

Takeaway. A single-error-correcting Hamming code spends one syndrome value on ‘no error’: m ≤ 2r − r − 1.
